Postulate

/POSS-chuh-layt/ - the stress falls on POSS · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Postulate means to assume something as a starting point for reasoning.

Euclid postulated that parallel lines never meet, then built two thousand years of geometry on the assumption.

Worked Example

Search planners postulate that a lost hiker drifts downhill and toward water. The rule is openly imperfect — some hikers climb — but adopting it lets the team rank the map's sectors within minutes instead of arguing all night.

Postulate is exact because the team did not claim the rule was true; they assumed it, deliberately and in the open, so reasoning could start. That is the word's whole job — a stated starting point. Posit would offer the rule for debate; postulate puts it to work.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

assume: To assume is to take something as true without noticing you have done it — casual, silent, unflagged. Postulate is the same move made openly and on purpose: the assumption is announced so everyone can see what the reasoning stands on. Assuming slips past; postulating is stated method.

presume: To presume is to believe something with more confidence than your evidence has earned, and to act as if it were settled. Postulate claims no belief at all: a postulated rule is adopted openly as a working basis, while a presumption quietly overreaches toward certainty.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

prove: to establish with evidence, so nothing is assumed

doubt: to withhold acceptance until the evidence arrives

Where it sits · how much certainty the claim carries — guess → postulate → establish

guess vs. postulate: A guess is weaker than a postulate — no structure, no plan, nothing built on it — while a postulate is adopted deliberately so reasoning can begin.

establish vs. postulate: Establish goes further than postulate: what you postulate you merely assume for the sake of the argument, while what you establish has been proven.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — postul

Root — postul: to demand, to claim (Latin postulare)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make, to do

Put it together

Put it together: Postul- (to demand, Latin postulare) + -ate = to claim something up front. A Roman postulare was a formal demand; scholars narrowed it to the one demand every argument makes — “grant me this to start with.” Note that the post- here is not the prefix meaning “after”; the resemblance is pure accident.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Postulate comes from Latin postulare, “to demand or claim” — later, “to claim as a basis for argument.” Outside this word and its noun twin, the root left almost no trace in English: its only cousin, postulant (a person formally requesting entry into a religious order), is rare. There is nothing here to peel off and reuse.

Strength Check

Word Choice

academic / technical

Postulate is at home in mathematics and science, where an assumption is adopted openly so reasoning can proceed. Posit, its neighbor in this unit, offers a claim for discussion; postulate installs one as a foundation. In casual speech, assume covers both.
